utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Yes, can I hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General Talic, good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED TALIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Yes, I can hear you in a language that I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You may sit down. Appearance for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, assisted by Hasan Younis, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman. I appear with Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic and Natasha Ivanovic-Fauveau for General Talic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Preliminaries before we start?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just this, Your Honour: We did a check yesterday on the three Sanski Most Rule 92 statements that you asked us about, and we confirmed that I think we did -- we did say it, as Mr. Ackerman pointed out at some stage, we're not going to call any of those witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And we're still considering the position of the one last witness from Sanski Most who couldn't come earlier. But we'll let Your Honours know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, as you know, we were handed some videotapes yesterday, and we've had a chance to review them, and either now or at a time when Ms. Korner might decide she wants to use them, we have some fairly serious objection to make to the use of any part of them. And when the Court wants to hear that, it is of course up to you all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I certainly will be applying to use it, whether with this witness or with one of the other witnesses who's coming. At the moment I'm hoping that we will have by the end of today a rough transcript in the Bosnian language of what's on the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's important, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As to translation, I don't know that -- I was hoping that we might be able to do it if the interpreters had the transcript in B/C/S, we might be able to get an instant translation over the headphones. But if there's to be an argument about it, certainly I will be applying to use what's on that tape. So obviously I'd like to call Mr. Filipovic this morning. He's been waiting to start his evidence. Maybe it's appropriate that we deal with it when we've got the transcript on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would say so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are we sitting in the mornings next month? I think we are, are we not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Next month we have a mixed -- I think the first week is in the afternoon. The second week is in the morning. The third week is in the afternoon. And I'm trying to make arrangements to have some further changes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I thought I'd -- when I looked at the list, we finally were being given morning sessions again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, it may have been changed because I made some representations earlier on this week.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the basis of the various complaints I was receiving and also because I feel that our case should not be treated any differently from other cases. And there should have been a further attempt at make some adjustments. But my secretary till yesterday, at least, did not inform me of any changes. As far as I know, next week is afternoons -- afternoon sittings, if I remember well. And the week after is morning sittings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, then, Your Honour, what I'll endeavour to do is to get sent to Your Honours the transcript -- of course that wouldn't help much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. What I would suggest -- what I would suggest is -- we don't have the video recording in any case as of yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You don't, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We haven't received it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If Mr. Ackerman would accept to give us some prior indication as to the basis of his objections.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then first of all, we can decide how best to go about it, because -- we could just hear the objections without having first seen the video recording. But definitely at least we will need to have an idea of what the video recording is all about. Or else get an indication of what the objections are likely -- are intended to be and then get the video recording from the Prosecution and see it ourselves, not in open session, and that would put us in a better position to be able to make an assessment and then we can discuss the whole -- the whole argument.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, then I wonder if -- I think that would help. And what I can try and do, if it's really necessary, I will try and persuade somebody to work overtime over the weekend to translate the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long do you anticipate Mr. Filipovic --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Filipovic to be here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, the best estimate -- I was talking to Defence counsel about that -- is I thought if he'd started yesterday, he would finish in chief on Monday. He's going to go through a number of the documents in the bundle as Your Honours saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this definitely -- if you're producing these two video recordings --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just one. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I make it absolutely clear, the second one we disclosed in case I might use. The one that I'm concerned about, that I want to use, is the one he brought. He's mentioned on it. I do know that. I've got a summary of what's on this video. It largely -- there's some interviews with a man called Vinko Kondic, who as Your Honours will hear was the chief of police. So effectively if Mr. Ackerman can indicate now very briefly so I can start the witness what the problem is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, unfortunately I don't understand the language myself either. But I think what would be -- what I would request -- and you of course may do whatever you wish -- is that you hear our objections before you have a chance to -- before you actually look at the tapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, of course. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Or read the transcripts of the tapes, because our view is they are wholly irrelevant, they are designed to foist propaganda upon you and have no -- they have no relevance whatsoever to any issue in this case. The one that she's talking about I think is a tape about bullfight where some people make some propagandistic speeches about how bad Serbs are.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I could be wrong about that. But I don't think there's anything relevant here. And to the extent that people speak on this tapes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Anyway --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, let me say this, Your Honour: To the extent that people speak on those tapes, I would certainly object to any of the actual speech being made record in this case unless cross-examination can be made. Because in effect they're going to be testifying in this case without any opportunity for us to cross-examine them. So maybe we will not object to the pictures being shown, but that remains to be seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, your, first of all let me say straight away there's -- absolutely -- Mr. Ackerman is absolutely right. At the beginning of this particular tape, there is a bullfight. Completely -- that is, of course, completely irrelevant, and it's not the parts that I intend to play. Later on in the tape there is, however, a segment which contains interviews -- and rightly -- Mr. Ackerman is quite right. It's propaganda. We say it is propaganda. And we say it is entirely and heavy relevant to this case -- from members of the Kljuc Crisis Staff, which include, as I say, Mr. Kondic, who Your Honours are going to hear a lot today from this witness, who was the chief of police; Mr. Bajic, who was also a member of the Kljuc Crisis Staff. And that's why we say this is utterly relevant. And there is, as I say -- as I understand it -- and all I have been given is a summary of what's on the tape -- a mention of Mr. Filipovic himself. And so we say it's highly relevant. And I don't see -- I'm not sure how Your Honours are going to decide whether it's relevant or not without knowing what the content is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We obviously have to know the content.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But Mr. Ackerman obviously is right in suggesting that first we should hear at least the basic argument before being able to -- to decide later. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But you can't hear a basic argument on relevance without knowing what -- that what's on the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At least we will know before why Mr. Ackerman and presumably also Mr. Zecevic believe that this whole -- this video recording in whole or in part may or may not be relevant. I mean, it's ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, can we do it this way then, that I will endeavour over the weekend to persuade somebody to earn overtime by translating what I hope will be a done transcript into English. And then if we could perhaps deal with that -- so it will be 2.15. And I will supply to Mr. Ackerman only to begin with them and to -- Mr. Zecevic doesn't need it in English. But if we have a transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then we can deal with it at 2.15. And if the witness could perhaps be told to come at quarter to 3, so he doesn't hang around on Monday. I know everybody here says they will be short, but I think half an hour probably is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if -- I'll make arrangements with Mr. Ackerman to meet him on Monday morning to give him what we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner, and I thank you Mr. Ackerman, Mr. Zecevic. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, Your Honour. I'm deeply grateful. Can I just remember something -- I'm deeply grateful to Mr. Younis who has reminded me of something. Could it be possible if Your Honour has a say about sittings in September/October, that Brdjanin/Talic sit at a different time to Stakic. In other words, if -- sit in the morning, we sit in the evening. Because we are going to be on Prijedor -- Stakic have been finishing off, although there have been delays for various reasons -- in September. But Judge Schomburg has set aside a week for -- I've forgotten what the word he used is. I think deliberations which are going to be held over the case. But counsel -- for example, Mr. Koumjian, who's largely been conducting that case and Ms. Sutherland will be calling the Prijedor witnesses, because it makes sense that they're called in that case. So it would help enormously if -- if on that particular -- for, say, a period of two weeks, from the 19th of September the Stakic sittings and the Brdjanin/Talic did not clash. In other words, both not sitting in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think those two weeks we are sitting in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Well, then I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Stakic alternates with Galic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And it may be easier, because they both use the same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I think -- as Your Honour recalls, we did make an attempt early on to try and combine the hearing of the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That didn't work. But I'd be very grateful -- this can't be that complicated I would hope to arrange for that period we would not be sitting at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we would have to deal -- Madam Registrar, will you please make note of that. And we'll try and deal with it either this afternoon or Monday morning first thing. Obviously we will have to consult with Judge Schomburg, who will definitely need to consult with -- yeah. We alternate with Simic most of the time. This month I think we are -- this month we are alternating with Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next month we would be with Simic. So I would -- we would need also to speak to Judge Mumba.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, may I suggest to you -- I mean, because from the information that I have just received, there may be a very simple solution to it. May I suggest to you to first thing Monday morning, because that's when it's more likely that we would know what the position is with regard to another trial that's going on, that -- yeah, and it's even -- I think we have got two solutions, not just one. I think we will be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm very grateful to Your Honour. That would really assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if I may -- if I may suggest to you to contact Madam Chuqing Monday morning, have someone contact her, so that we'll give this matter our utmost attention. I am to assume that there's no objection forthcoming from the Defence. I'm sure you would prefer to have a shifting -- yeah. Okay. Thanks. Thank you, usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome back to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are about to start giving evidence in this case. And before you do so, our Rules require that you enter a solemn declaration that in the course of your testimony you will be telling us the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of this solemn declaration is contained on a piece of paper that the usher will hand to you. And may I kindly ask you to make that solemn declaration by reading that statement, solemn declaration, aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is your commitment with this Tribunal. This is equivalent to an oath. In other words, you are bound to tell us the truth and the whole truth. You may sit down. And let me explain to you very briefly what's going to happen. First of all, as you see, you're sitting in a courtroom. And we are the three Judges composing this Trial Chamber. My name is Agius and I come from Malta. To my right is my colleague Judge Janu from the Czech Republic and to my left is Judge Taya from Japan. The three persons sitting in front of us are the members of the Registry. And to your immediate right you see two persons. And that is the team for the Prosecution. Ms. Korner, Joanna Korner, with whom you are already familiar, will be the person that will be conducting the examination-in-chief. In other words, she will be asking you a set of questions which you are bound, obliged to answer unless we stop you. That is your duty. We will stop Ms. Korner if there is a valid objection or if we think that you should not answer a particular question. When the examination-in-chief by the Prosecutor will be concluded -- is concluded, then you will be cross-examined by the two Defence teams. And the two Defence teams are to your left. In the front row there is the Defence team for Radoslav Brdjanin, one of the accused in this trial; and in the back row there are -- there is the Defence team for General Talic, who is also -- who is the other accused in this trial. As I tried to explain to you earlier, the same applies when you are -- the same rule applies when you are being cross-examined by the Defence counsel. The two Defence counsel will be doing their duty here towards their clients. They have a right to cross-examine you, and therefore your reciprocal obligation, duty, is to answer all the questions that are put to you by the Defence unless we tell you not to answer, unless we stop you. Having said that, I now leave you not hands of Ms. Korner, who will start with her examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before I begin, can I take it that Your Honour will be sitting until 10.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then there will be a break at 10.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The break will be a little bit shorter today, since we are stopping at 12.00, 12.15.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour -- yes, I wonder if the ELMO could just be moved away slightly for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Usher, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's a bit difficult. That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, is your name Muhamed Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were you born on the 27th of October, 1955 in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And are you a Bosniak, a Bosnian Muslim, by nationality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a number of questions -- just wait -- about your life and the events of 1992. But if I may, I want to encapsulate it, first of all. I think it's right that by 1992 you were a married man with a son.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you were and still are a surveyor by profession.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it's also right that you had a brother, Omer Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I had a brother. I do not have a brother. My brother was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's your brother who was the Omer Filipovic who was killed in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The encapsulation that I'm talking about went as follows, I think: That you were taken prisoner by the Serbs in May of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That you went to Banja Luka, first of all, to Banja Luka police station -- I'm sorry, to Kljuc police station.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then to Banja Luka to Mali Logor.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: From there to Stara Gradiska.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And eventually did you end up in Manjaca yourself?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were you one of the people who was airlifted out of Manjaca as a result of a Red Cross relief operation?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you end up in England?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I did. I came to England to be treated because I was severely ill. And owing to the services of the International Red Cross, I was transferred to England for treatment, where I underwent four surgical operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you remain in England until after the Dayton Accords had been signed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then eventually did you return to Kljuc, where you've remained?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And just so the Court understands, I think it's right that you understand some English, although perhaps with less facility in speaking.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can understand it. I can't really speak it. But as far as I need it, it's quite enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, although the Court has heard some evidence relating to events in Kljuc, I want to deal a little bit with the municipality of Kljuc itself, since you, I think, lived there all your life. First of all, I'd like you to have a look, please, at a map of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, which was Exhibit P446.1.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if we could have that put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is really just to identify its positioning within the Autonomous Region. We can see that Kljuc was -- I'm going to get this wrong, I think -- south-east of Banja Luka -- south-west? No. South-west. I've got it wrong, have I? Yeah, south-west of Banja Luka. It borders with Sanski Most to the top and then to Kljuc -- I'm sorry, to Bosanski Petrovac to the west. And we can see marked on it - and we'll have a closer look at a bigger map - the various ethnicities that were in the villages. As a municipality, Mr. Filipovic, did Kljuc have any particular strategic importance that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In my opinion, the municipality of Kljuc was very important strategically speaking for Bosnia-Herzegovina from a historical perspective, because in Kljuc the very last Bosnian king died after the Turks were conquering Bosnia, and it was in Kljuc that Bosnia had fallen. And in my personal opinion, the people who wanted to destroy Bosnia believed that if Kljuc was destroyed, that Bosnia would be destroyed, because in the Middle Ages Kljuc was one of the capitals of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we now look, please, at the ethnic make-up of the municipality. And can you briefly please be shown what was Exhibit P60.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And again, if that could be put on the ELMO in the English version and Mr. Filipovic get the version in the Bosnian language. And usher, if you just give it to me, I'll just get the right place. Thanks. Or actually, it's all in the Bosnian language, so it doesn't make much difference. Yeah. It is actually -- I don't think we got -- we didn't get it translated, I don't think. So we'll just put it on the ELMO. Your Honour, this is page 19 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This document is the results of the census that were taken in 1971, 1981, and 1991. If we look at Kljuc, the population between 1971 and 1991 dropped from -- the total population -- 39.966 to 37.391. And then if we look at the number of Croats, there were 534 in 1971 and 330 in 1991. For the Muslims, 15.226 in 1971, and it had grown to 17.696 by 1991. And for the Serbs, 23.892 in 1971 and 18.508 in 1991. And there were a few what were called -- people who described themselves as Yugoslavs in 1991 and who described themselves as others. Now, if we look at the proportions, we can see that the Croats formed .9 per cent of the population in 1991, the Muslims 47.3, and the Serbs 49.5 per cent. There was a decrease apparently in the number of Serbs from 1971. Are you aware of the explanation for that, Mr. Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The last three censuses I can comment in the following way: In 1971, it was for the first time that in the former Yugoslavia, that is, in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that there was a census when the Bosnian Muslims, that is, Muslims in Bosnia, were recognised as a nationality, and they were allowed to register themselves as Muslims. And it was from then on that that part of Yugoslav peoples were either -- until then were either Serbs, Croats, or not determined. But it was after 1971, that is, for the first time in 1971 that there was the possibility that they had a right for them as a population to register as Muslims. I believe that it was then that out of fear and out of dilemma as to what will happen in the future with them they still did not register themselves in that census as Muslims. And that is why we see the tendency of an increase in 1971, 1981, 1991 that the Muslim population has been increasing, that is, that the more the Yugoslav state was democratised, the more people ceased to be fearful and they were able to say what they felt. As for the Serbs and as for their rapid decrease in the census, I can say that Serbs were leaving en masse in the direction of Serbia. There was a continuous movement and started from 1945, because there was a colonisation of Vojvodina that was ongoing and practically all Serbs from the Kljuc municipality were going to Vojvodina. And there were -- they went to live there. And this was almost an unwritten rule, unwritten law that if a father had, say, four sons, three would go to Vojvodina and one would remain in Bosnia. One would remain on their land in Bosnia, while three of them would receive a land in Vojvodina. So in this way from 1945 onwards the Serbs were -- could simply say that Vojvodina was nationally speaking Serbian, although historically speak Vojvodina was never Serbian until 1945.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We can take that document away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And could you now have a look, please, at a map that's been prepared which just show it is municipality of Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a new map. A copy, I think, was provided to the registry, this one. And I'd ask that it then be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 1097.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, if you can see that --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, we can come back slightly so that Mr. Filipovic can see the whole map. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a map that's been prepared, which I think you've had a chance to look at, Mr. Filipovic, which shows the various -- or some of the villages within Kljuc itself by ethnicity. And would you agree that that is if not 100 per cent accurate, roughly accurate of how the ethnicities, the nationalities, were divided?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: This question, if Your Honours will allow me, I can just add one more comment. I can say that I agree, although I would add, if Your Honours will allow me, just to say that in very recent past in Rastoka, Orahovljani and here I cannot see Sredice and Zablace, they were -- villages including Sitnica where Muslims formed a majority in the Kljuc municipality. Sredice perhaps is not here, because it belongs to Grebnik [phoen]. So these villages that are mentioned from the Second World War onwards were villages from which Muslims were forced out, and so they went to villages around Kljuc. But this current situation on this map fully is in line with the way population was distributed in the municipality of Kljuc until 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So effectively we can see that the Muslim-type villages were closest really to Sanski Most; is that right? The ones closest to Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. In 1962 there was a reform of the establishment of the then-Kljuc municipality. It cannot be seen on this map. Two large villages were taken off from the -- or taken out of the Kljuc municipality. They were 100 per cent Muslim. And they were attached to the Sanski Most municipality only for the reason so that it can be manipulated so that the Kljuc municipality would turn out to be of Serb municipality. And these were Hrustovo and Vrhpolje. What I mean is that until 1962, these two villages were -- belonged to the municipality of Kljuc. And if there was this proportion of population, then we could not at all be talking about a majority of the Serb population in the Kljuc municipality. We would only be talking about the majority Muslim population because Hrustovo itself and Vrhpolje had about 10.000 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you could put that away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then finally I'd like you to have a look at a map of the town of Kljuc itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, it's a new exhibit, which I think has been handed to Your Honours and the Court. And may it be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 1098. Your Honour, it contains photographs without a legend.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is a plan of the town of Kljuc itself, Mr. Filipovic, which again you've had an opportunity to look at. First of all, within the town, were there certain areas that were Serb and certain that were Muslim, or was it a mixed population within the town?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: This question I could answer in the following way: By the earthquake in Banja Luka -- until the earthquake in Banja Luka in 1969, the Kljuc was populated 90 per cent by Muslim population, Bosnian population. After the earthquake in Banja Luka in 1969, there was a sudden change of population from the surrounding villages, Ribnik, Sitnica. There were a large number of Serb inhabitants came to live in the town of Kljuc. They populated the town, only the actual urban area of Kljuc, while all peripheral settlements of Kljuc -- we can see Tomasevica Grad -- this is the old part of town where the last Bosnian king Stjepan Tomasevic lived. And other settlements. On the other side Bebici, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch all the names of the settlements.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Filipovic. Could you stop for a moment. It's very important that you don't go too fast. And the interpreter didn't catch some of the names that you mentioned. I'll tell you what, if you can -- we'll bring the ELMO towards you, and if you can indicate with a pointer that you'll be given the areas that you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Here, in the northern part we can see Tomasevica Grad. This is the old part of town, dating from Roman times where the last Bosnian king lived Stjepan Tomasevic. Below the town itself there is the village of Bebici or the locality of Bebici, which is 100 per cent Muslim populated. On the other side of the Sana River is the settlement of Mehmedagici. This is not in this part of map. You cannot see it. But it is below the old town, Stjepan Tomasevic town. And it is on the other side of the Sana River, because here question see the Sip factory. And from the other side we can see the Mehmedagici locality. To my knowledge, there was only one Serb family in the last 47 years. Now, on the other side, vis-a-vis we are going in a southerly direction from Mehmedagici locality. There is a locality that we used to call Sarica Brdo. And there is also not very -- there are not very many inhabitants. These are mostly Muslims. Now, in the westerly direction, we come what has been -- called Zelica Brdo and until then was populated by Muslims. But it is actually known as Handanovica Brdo. The older inhabitants of the Kljuc town was known as Handanovica Brdo because Handanovici Muslims lived there. Further on, in the westerly direction, there is the hamlet of Hanlovici, 100 per cent Muslim. If we go further in the westerly direction we come to the locality of Rejzovici, also 100 per cent Muslim population. Going out of Kljuc is the hamlet of Velagici. So this is north-west. And it is also populated by Muslims. Then if we go towards the north and towards the Tomasevica Grad, there is the locality of Sehici, 100 per cent Muslim. What I mean to say is that all of the surrounding area of Kljuc town is almost 100 per cent Muslim, while in the town itself, the town of Kljuc, in the centre, as you say in England, it is mixed population. It is mixed population, and we cannot say where Serbs are, where Muslims are. But in the town itself we believe that it is half and half. So you cannot say which of the two is the majority, because the Serb who is have 2 per cent majority, this is because the villages of Vrbljani and Ribnik. Numerically speaking, they have advantage over the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, thank you very much. Now, just before you leave the map, can you indicate to the Court where you lived?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Here. Here in this part is my house where my father lived, my great-grandfather. My father came from -- great-grandfather came from Sredice. And my grandfather came from in 1978 [As interpreted] -- when he was forced out, Sredice used to be ours, but to date we have never been given any compensation, not a penny. This has been taken away from us. And this is where I used to live, in the immediate vicinity. This -- I don't know whether Your Honours can see it. This house here, this is the house which I sold to my best friend Vinko Kondic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So -- usher, could you please give the witness a coloured pen. And could the witness please mark on the map with an "X" and then the -- his residence, his home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether this is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Could you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's -- that's where your home is though. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you put an "H" on top of that "X," please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And perhaps you could also indicate where you say Vinko Kondic's home was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: With a "K."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The house you sold to Vinko Kondic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you mark it on the map with a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would use a different colour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Use a different colour. Don't worry. I will please you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If he could be given a different -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And put a "K," please, on top of that cross.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Now, in the space to the right, could you just put your initials, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's enough. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to say that I did not sell Vinko Kondic a house. I sold him a plot of land where he then built a house. I sold him a land, plot of land.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, then finally before we leave this map, can we just look at some of the photographs that are there. The top photograph, can you tell us what that represents, the one marked "1."

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: This is the health centre in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The hospital. And we can see that indicated on the map. Ignore, please, 2 and 3, because those are areas as opposed to -- well, you may be able -- can you tell us -- you may be able to tell what you say number 2 represents. If you can't, say so straight away.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: This is some derelict house. I cannot determine the location. But these are derelict houses. I cannot tell you exactly where they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. That's fine. Could you then go, please, to photograph number 4. And could you tell us what that is.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the microphone of the witness please be adjusted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just a moment. Pause. The microphone -- if you could pull up that microphone so the interpreters can hear him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what number 4 represents.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: This is the building of the Kljuc municipality. This building here is where I had worked 1992, the very last window here, where I worked until 1992. And the fourth window to the right is the window of the office where I work now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So that's the municipality building in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it's been marked on the map, Your Honours. As "municipal assembly." But I don't think there's any dispute it's one in the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Number 5, can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: This is the building of the primary school in Kljuc. Before the war it was known as Nikola Mackic. And then in 1992 in the sports hall of the school, where you can just see the corner, in the latter part of the school the Serb extremist carried out detention and beatings of Muslims and Croats. This was like a collection point where they were collecting people before they were taking them to -- before they took them to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Photograph number 6, are you able to identify that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: This is a football pitch, the stadium of the football club Kljuc. This is a container where drinks are sold at halftime. And in 1992 when I was captured, women and children and all other Muslims and Croats who happened to be in Kljuc and who were not taken to Manjaca, they were brought there. This is where a selection was carried out where men were divided from women and children and men were later on deported to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's been indicated, your, as "sports field," but I think the description is the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Number 7, please, if you can help us.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Photograph number 7 is part of the cultural centre where sociopolitical organisations. The left-hand side of the photograph there is a cinema, a theatre hall, and so on. The lower part is the town library. And then in this other part is where political parties were based, where they are located.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Number 8?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Photograph number 8 is the police administration in Kljuc, where I was held. And now these steps are slightly changed from those before. They used to be old staircase of the police administration. And we the prisoners, specifically myself, we were thrown from this part here, when they forced me to go to Stara Gradiska, they threw me from there to there to the bottom of the stairs with my hands tied behind my back. I tumbled down the staircase all the way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Number 9, I'm not sure that you'll be able to help with, but if you can, you tell us in 1992 what was there.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can, because I know what this is. The white part of the building up to here. So this white part is the municipal hall of Kljuc. And the red part is the building which housed the Territorial Defence in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And they are adjoining buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then finally, number 10?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The Orthodox church, which is in the very heart of Kljuc. After the liberation of Kljuc, it survived, unlike 17 mosques and the Catholic church, which were all destroyed in 1992. Yet the Orthodox church is still standing in Kljuc, and nothing is wrong with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. And now, finally, before we leave it, we've heard there were very few Croats living in the Kljuc municipality. Were there Croats living in Kljuc town itself?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, of the figure that we could see concerning the last census, which showed that there were 330 Croats. I'd say that half of them lived in the town and another half in the locality of Velagici and perhaps in Oraskovici [phoen] or perhaps somebody lived in Sanica. But those would be individual cases to groups you would find in Velagici and Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You can leave the map now. You can take that away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you a little bit about to the background of the events of 1992. First of all, could you tell us a little bit, please, about your brother, Omer. What was his position within the community of Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Prior to the first multi-party elections, my late brother Omer was taught [As interpreted] at the Lazar Djukic secondary school in Kljuc. Following the first multi-party elections, my late brother founded a party, the SDA. And after that, the party called MBO, and then he tried to organise all the population structures which agreed with his political positions. So in the first multi-party political elections he participated in the elections, and there we tried to work on our own, because we did not enjoy the support of the authorities. In contrast with other parts which existed there, which enjoyed the support of the official authorities. For instance, the SDS had agreed you will be in the League of Communists. You've got the power, but you will be helping us. We did not have that. We had to finance ourselves for the first multi-party elections, and we won 20 seats. The SDA won 16; MBO won 4. And the Municipal Assembly of Kljuc at that time had 61 seats, which means that we won almost one-third of the power there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can you pause for a moment, because I'm going to come on to the multi-party elections. I just want to deal for a moment with Omer's position. You said he founded a party called -- you say he founded the -- I didn't think you said the SDA. Did you say the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. You did. Right. So he was one of the founding members of the SDA and then founded a party called the MBO.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, can you tell us what the initials --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He didn't say that he was one of the founding members of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, he never --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He said that he founded the SDA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Those are Ms. Korner's words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- I recall the witness saying precisely what Mr. Ackerman has brought out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour. I said that first. And then I'm sorry if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's all right. It's all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Slightly a change in --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. First of all the -- let's deal with that. The SDA. You say he founded the SDA. Where did he found the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. In Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The Kljuc SDA. Not the Bosnian SDA. The Kljuc SDA.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Then you say that he founded another party called the MBO. Can you just tell the Court what the MBO stood for, the initials.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Muslim Bosniak Organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And why did he found a separate party from the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Personally because he thought that only people with a number of political parties is a proper political people, that is, not to have a one-track political mind, to think only along the lines of one party, but let people think whatever they like and then opt for whichever party they like.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was there any major difference between the platform, that is, the ideas or the things that were said, between the SDA and the MBO at the time of the 1990 elections?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: No major difference. The chief difference was that the SDA held -- that we were Muslims by ethnicity and the MBO considered all inhabitants of Bosnia-Herzegovina where Bosniaks -- but Bosniak Catholics, Bosniak Orthodox, Bosniak Muslims. Otherwise they agreed that the Bosnian border should be the avnoj, borders, and everything else -- other parties and other problematic -- were the same. That that was the only difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the MBO was founded before the 1990 election.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is why we could participate in the elections. Had it been founded after the election, it wouldn't be able to take part in the elections.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Who was the leader, then, of the SDA in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: To the founding convention, when my brother founded the SDA, he said "Then from the days now, I turn over the place of the president to Mr. Asim Egrlic, and now I set off to found another political party."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you yourself, did you stand in the 1990 elections as a candidate?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And for which of the two parties?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The MBO.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Up till then, had you had any involvement in politics?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Why, no. I wasn't politically active until 1990, except that in Bosnia we had such a system. Until 1987 I was a member of the League of Communists, because we had a single-party system. You had to be a member of the league, and I was a member of the league. And for a while I was a secretary of the basic organisation in the municipality that I worked in. But I don't see it as some kind of -- it was no kind of political activity. It's simply something that came from the head office, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what made you stand for election as a candidate?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: One of the chief reasons for my nomination was that I was present, and I believe it was October 1st in the restaurant called Lane across the street from the Orthodox church was -- the SDS held it founding convention. And at that time I was a citizen who attended all -- I still attend everything, so I was listening to the speeches of all the speakers who were in the garden of that restaurant on days. And one of them was my great friend until that time, Vinko Kondic. When I heard what Vinko Kondic was saying at the founding convention of the SDS, and Vinko Kondic has spent more time in my house and I spent more time in his -- in our own respective houses -- then I told myself, Well, if Vinko can say this, who is a lawyer, who is an educated man, who with me and my brother Omer and Dule, the four of us were like four brothers, then what can I expect from somebody from Sredice, from somebody from Rakovica who only attends to his sheep. So Muhamed, listen if Vinko can be a great Serb, then you can be a great Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pause please.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And that was when I decided to join the politics.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. What was it that Vinko was saying that provoked this reaction in you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, almost as far as I can remember, because it was a long time ago. It was 12 years ago practically. But I remember hey him saying that they would be biologically danger. That in the territory of Bosnia, especially in Krajina, the Serbs were threatened with biological extermination, that they had been brought to those territories, and there was nobody there. That they had no jobs. Look around you, look how rich the Muslims are, see how we have nothing. And he refused to face the reality. He refused to go back to the '60s when the Muslims in Kljuc could not get a job but had to go to Germany, to Switzerland, or to the Netherlands. The situation changed and the mark dollar, Dule, began to be worth something. Then they began to lose its value. Those who lived there were simply making their ends meet, but they had fought for it. They had worked. And these were bothered by it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just watching the transcript and listening, I think the translator and the court reporter are having a very difficult time creating proper transcript here because the witness is talking so very rapidly. I just think they are having a very hard time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you for bringing that up, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Filipovic, could I kindly ask you to slow down because we have -- here we have interpreters translating to us from your language to French and to English, and they have to catch up with every single word that you say. So if you slow down a little bit, you would be helping them tremendously.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I will do my best. I will try to speak slower. But for the past 12 years, since the war broke out, these -- they forced me to speak faster. Now you tell me to speak slower, but I'll do my best to speak slower.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we just leave -- the interpreters are, may I saying, to the greatest respect to Mr. Ackerman, are capable of telling us to ask the witness to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you told us about what Vinko Kondic was saying, and as a result of that you've told us you decided to stand for election. For which party -- I'm sorry, you -- I think you did tell us. You told us you stood for the MBO. Were you elected?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I was. But before that there on the days was also my late brother at the founding convention because they had invited him as a guest and he was there, quite in the immediate neighbourhood of Radovan Karadzic. And my brother then stepped out on behalf of the Muslims of Kljuc. He spoke and said, "Thank you, Serbs. You've organised yourselves today. You've made it possible for us to organise ourselves because you were the first ones to start this. It will be easier for me to organise my people now." But I was so indignant after Vinko's address. I was waving to Omer and saying, "Give me the application card, because from now on I will be with you, because until the -- for the month before that, I was telling Omer, 'Oh, get away with this politics. I mean, I don't want to do anything with it.'"

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And in the elections I was elected as one of four MBO candidates.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And I think you told us a little earlier that the number of people elected was -- for the parties was as follows: That your party, the MBO, received 4 seats.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The SDA achieved 16, and the SDS 31.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then I think there were another 10 seats which were allocated between different smaller parties.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: At that time they were called -- I think it was the SDP, and that was the successor to the League of Communists. Then the Reformist's party. Then there was another one. I believe there were four of them. I can't really give you the names of these parties, but I believe there were four parties and they had ten deputies altogether.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please come closer to the microphone or speak up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm afraid this is -- you'll learn, I'm afraid, over the next few days. The interpreters are asking if you could lean towards the microphone or perhaps bring your chair in so they can hear you. So therefore the result, I think, was that the SDS had an overall majority within the assembly of one seat.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. Yes. Yes. They had the majority, and whatever decision required relative majority, they could do it by themselves without any other party. They could take whatever decision in the municipal assembly in Kljuc. Of course some other decisions required two thirds majority. And then they tried to make some calculations. After 1990, after the elections, they could function by themselves, since they had one-third [As interpreted] Of the seats in the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But at the same time I think there were elections to the assembly in Sarajevo. And I would like you just very briefly, please, to have a look at a document, the gazette, which recorded the result of that election.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could the witness be handed P758B. It's the gazette in B/C/S. And we'll have the English put on the ELMO. And again, if the usher could give it to me first. I'll find the relevant bits.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think we can deal with this fairly briefly, Mr. Filipovic. In the election to the national assembly in Sarajevo, was a Serb who we're going to hear more about, called Rajko Kalabic elected?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. He won. He won because Dr. Mesic Suad was running against him, but Rajko Kalabic won more votes and went to represent the SDS in the Bosnian parliament.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, you can take that document away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you've -- before I move on to what happened after the elections, you've told us about your friendship with Vinko Kondic. What were relations like between the nationalities up until and indeed so after the elections?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, up to 1990, up to the first multi-party elections, and even for a goodish part of -- that is, the elections took place in November. So for the first half of 1991, this nationalistic wave did not swell that much in the municipality of Kljuc, so it was quite natural for a Muslim Serb, a Croat, to go to a tavern together, order drinks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the interpretation is coming in very feint in my case, at least. I can barely hear the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If Your Honour maybe turns up the volume on the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't touched it. Can I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: One, two, three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. You were saying that it was quite natural for a Muslim, a Serb, a Croat to go to a tavern together and order drinks. Was there intermarriage between the various nationalities?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Why, yes. Specifically I have some relatives who are in mixed marriages. And Vinko Kondic, his brother Dule is a Muslim, that is, Vinko's sister-in-law is a Muslim. In Bosnia you can hardly find those areas where people are not mixed, whether Muslim and Serb, Serb and Croat. I mean, it's all mixed. Mr. Izetbegovic used to say, "Bosnia-Herzegovina is like leopard skin." I mean, it's all so mixed that it's impossible to really separate individual ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us, however, that one of the factors or maybe the factor that made you stand for election was the speech made by Vinko Kondic in respect of the Serbs being threatened.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Had speeches like that been made before the elections, or was that the first time that you heard those type of speeches, of that type of speech?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I heard this speech delivered by my best friend. Before that I've heard other speeches of that kind, but I wasn't interested in them. But because the men who delivered the speech was my friend with whom I'd drunk up tonnes of water together [As interpreted], loaves of bread together, it hurt me to hear it from him, not when I heard it from some other Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, just very briefly, because I want to go back to what happened in the assembly after the elections. When did relationships between the various nationalities really here in Kljuc, between the Muslims and the Serbs, begin to deteriorate badly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: As I have said, up to the elections. And -- but the deterioration -- things started to deteriorate when the Serb extremists took over the repeat of the Sarajevo Radio Television on Kozara and started using it to transmit the channel 2 of the Belgrade television. That is when the relations became exacerbated. If the Court will allow me, I will tell you a joke which I used to tell at that time because I was never afraid to tell jokes or say what I think. So if I am permitted ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think that unless it really illustrates, Mr. Filipovic, what you -- what you're trying to explain, I think not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me -- let's hear it. Let's hear it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps you'll make our day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I used to say -- in the morning we would get to work, so we're having our morning coffee, Serbs and Muslims together, commenting on the previous evening's events. And I said, "Listen, folks. If I continue watching the Belgrade television, I'll become a greater Chetnik than you are." What I'm trying to say is what these programmes did -- hatred in among -- in the Serb people against other peoples. We heard fairy tales, myths. Bones were taken out of different pits, saying that these were Serb bones only and nobody else's, as if no other citizen of the then-Yugoslavia had ever perished. So I think that the chief inducer of this inter-ethnic intolerance was channel 2 of the Belgrade television, but I can't really remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we've heard other evidence this was August 1991, Mr. Filipovic. And finally, before the break, can I just ask you this and get it out of the way: Who was Professor Muhamed Filipovic, who had the same name as you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor Muhamed Filipovic had relatives. He had one particular relative who, in the elections of 1990, was a member of the state parliament. He was one of the presidents of the MBO. During the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina he was Bosnia-Herzegovina's ambassador to Switzerland and the UK. Currently lives in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think I know what Mr. Zecevic is going to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just explain, Mr. Filipovic, what relationship, if any, did you have with him?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean? We were related.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But how? Was he a cousin, brother, uncle?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: His and my grandfather are brothers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, do you still have --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I was just making an intervention in the transcript, because the witness has said that they were relatives, and it says Professor Filipovic had relatives.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I noticed that. I thought that can't be right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. Everything is okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm getting a fairly long list of transcript problems, and I don't know when you want to go through them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Unless -- unless any of them is highly critical, which needs to be clarified before the witness moves ahead, then we'll leave them today end. But perhaps now that we are going to break, if you have -- how many of them do you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Five.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I do hope -- you know, it -- I do hope that they really are critical, because basically we -- we should be depending on the interpreters and not on what counsel thinks was said or should be corrected. We're going to get terrible problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. Okay. But let's see what they are. Come on, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We should have an accurate transcript, Your Honour. And that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Line 19 -- page 19, line 8, the transcript says 1991. The witness said "1992."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page 19 you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 19, line 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When you were being asked to give information based on the map of Kljuc municipality that you were being shown, you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- You mentioned -- and here I cannot see, for example, Zablace, which is on the map incidentally. I mean, you didn't see it, but it is there. There were villages including -- where Muslims formed the majority in the Kljuc municipality. Zablace is not there because perhaps it belongs to Gornji Ribnik. So these mentioned from the Second World War were villages in which Muslims were forced out and so they went to villages around Kljuc. But this current situation on this map fully is in line with the way population was distributed in the municipality of Kljuc until 1991. Did you say "until 1991" or "until 1992"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until the census of 1991. Otherwise 1992. But the census was in 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next one, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's page 22, line 21. There's -- it's all quite confused, but I'm told that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page 22, line ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 21, where it says 1978, I'm told he said 1878.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where you mentioned that your grandfather came from Srednice. When did he come from --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1878.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1878. That's essentially before. Okay. Next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Line -- page 27, line 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When talking about his brother, he said -- the transcript says his brother was taught. And what he said was his brother was a teacher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That can be accepted. Go ahead. Next.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 37, line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is something that could be corrected later, Mr. Ackerman. I mean, it's -- it's so obvious, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So we'll break for 20 minutes. Twenty minutes from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, just before we go back to the assembly and the elections, I just want to deal briefly- and I should have dealt with it earlier - with the statements you made -- that you've made before you came here to testify. Can you just confirm the following: You were originally seen by a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor in -- give me -- I'll just check the date -- May of 1997. You may not remember the dates, but you remember being seen by an investigator?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely, as far as the date is concerned, I don't know. But yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then in May of 2000, I think you made a statement to a member of AID in Bosnia, a Mr. Ibric.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were seen again by the Office of the Prosecutor in March of 2001.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And made a further statement as a result of being seen the day before yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then the last document, which I will call a "statement," although in inverted commas. Did you in July of 1992 when at Manjaca sign a document?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And I will deal with the Manjaca one at a later stage. Now, can we go back, please, to the assembly. You've given us the results of the election. Can you tell us how the various positions, such as the chairman of the executive council, police, and the like were allocated after the elections. To which parties did the major posts go?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: There was -- since the SDS after the elections in 1990, it was -- they won. In Kljuc they undertook to divide the power with the thesis that when we came to negotiate between the parties, who's going to get what, in the authorities the SDS representatives said they had to have the police, the army, post office, finance, that is, they took over all the institutions of power which have decisive power, which was military, police, and money. And then the other sectors were given to the other parties in order so they can negotiate what can be had by whom.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. First of all, who became the president of the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: President of the Kljuc assembly, following the first multi-party elections, was Jovo Banjac, a civil engineer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Vice-president?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Vice-president was my late brother, Omer Filipovic, because the statute of the Kljuc municipality was such that if in one management position or leadership position there is a man of Serb nationality, his deputy should be a Muslim, or the other way round, which means the president was -- if the president had been a Muslim, then the deputy would have been a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who became the president of the executive council?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Asim Egrlic, an architect.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What position did Mr. Vinko Kondic hold immediately after the elections?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Following at the recollections, he was the secretary of the municipal assembly of the Kljuc municipality for a short while and then he became chief of police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, up until the outbreak of the war in Croatia, did matters function at the assembly on a reasonably amicable level between the parties?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Everything went normally unless there was something on the agenda in relation to town planning. And this town planning was a problem because this is something where people had to support each other, because in the town planning that's how people got rewarded, people who obey the authorities, they managed -- certain people managed to get some locations that were not allowed in town planning. But through certain connections these decisions could be changed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did that have anything to do with inter-ethnic rivalry or conflict, or was it purely, as it were, a matter that perhaps really, I suppose, one could call corruption?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Personally I think that this was more a problem of conflict between nationalities or ethnicities, because Serbs got something that Muslims for 30, 40 years could not have, and Serbs would get that overnight. Overnight they would get building permission. Even if from time immemorial, this would be, for instance, a Muslim plot. People were forced to sell their land to Serbs in order to get a permission. A specific example, myself. In my land I sold a plot to Vinko so that my brother and I would get building permissions, because Vinko got a permission so we had to get one, although this happened before the elections.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to trace the events of 1991 through -- or rather, with the help of some of the documents that we've recovered. I would like you, please, to be shown the documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is in volume 1 of the three binders. And it's been already pre-marked. And this, I don't think, can be right. It's the one behind divider 9. But it's got a -- it looks like it says Exhibit P3, but that I don't think can be right from my copy. It is -- Your Honour, yes, it is P3. Oh, I know why, because it was one of the ones that was looked at by Mr. -- Dr. Donia. But it's the second document behind divider -- in the bundle behind divider 9. And could he be handed, please -- yes, it had an original number of P851 until we suddenly realised it was already exhibited. Now, could we have the English on the ELMO, please, and -- there's not massive interest, I see, from the public -- and if Mr. Filipovic could have the original, which I'd invite Your Honours to look at, because I'm afraid that again something has been missed out of the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a document which begins: "Despite the fact that the Kljuc Municipal Assembly confirmed its existence," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But Your Honour, in the original, one can see quite clearly that it says "On the 10th of April, 1991," and that's been omitted from the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This document begins -- and I'll just read the beginning and then I'll ask you about the part of it. "Despite the fact that the Kljuc Municipal Assembly --" and I think it must say "on the 10th of April, 1991 -- "confirms its existence and further participation in the Banja Luka community of Municipalities and that it has elected its representatives to the Community Assembly, due to the previous transformation of this community into a regional community of 'Bosanska Krajina' and subsequently into the Autonomous Region of 'Bosanska Krajina' of the recently conducted plebiscite of the Serbian people and especially due to the fact that the municipal board of the MBO continues to deny the membership of the Kljuc municipality in the Regional Community, it is hereby proposed that the municipal assembly adopts the following decision at its session today:" Now, before I come to the decision, it is clear that this document, although it refers to the 10th of April in the original, must have been brought into existence after November of 1991 because of the reference to the plebiscite. But first of all, can you tell us about the Banja Luka Community of Municipalities, the involvement of the Kljuc Municipal Assembly with that organisation.
