utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: We -- when I say "we," I mean municipality of Kljuc, we were part of the community of the Municipalities of Jajce, and with all of these municipalities, we belonged to Jajce. And then there was a change following the elections. There was a change, and from the municipality of Kljuc it was asked to leave the community of Jajce municipalities and to join the Community of Municipalities of Banja Luka. We, belonging to the Muslim people, that is, SDA and MBO party members, in an unwritten agreement with the SDS members we accepted this at first, that Kljuc should join the Banja Luka region. We even once gave our own representative. And at one of these sessions my late brother attended. But we never accepted to be part of the Autonomous Region of Bosnian Krajina. And the main conflict between us and the SDS in Kljuc was becoming part of the Serbian -- Serb Autonomous Region of Krajina, which we opposed, and then the Serbs -- when I say "Serbs," I mean the SDS authorities in Kljuc -- they adopted such decisions which were supposed to satisfy the authorities in Banja Luka, that is, Mr. Brdjanin and his associates, and they sent this decision. And anyone normal would see that if a official document is forwarded, it should with registered. It should be under a certain number. But this just passed through in my own opinion, my own personal assessment -- I cannot tell you for sure because I don't have access to complete documentation. But this just went through the structures of the executive board of the SDS, and they put the seal of the Bosnia-Herzegovina state. And at that time, as far as the authorities -- the Serb authorities, there was a duplicity involved. Wherever they needed Bosnia-Herzegovina, then they would put that as being valid, this seal of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And if they needed something else, then they would put their own seal, "Serb Autonomous Region of Bosnian Krajina," or something like that. So Your Honours, you will see in many cases there will be a Bosnian seal and then there would be a different seal. This, in my opinion, this was a greater source of conflict about what Omer was doing as vice-president and what Mr. Banjac was doing. You cannot work like this. This did not go through the session. He's calling upon the session held on the 10th of April, 1991. But in order to confirm this, he has got to have a proper document which would say "according to decision of such and such a number."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we take this in two stage, because although it's clear that the document refers to the decision on the 10th of April, 1991, it must have come into existence later, because it also refers to the plebiscite of the Serbian people. But I want to concentrate for a moment on this -- the document itself. It bears a stamp, you tell us, of the Bosnian -- of -- or a seal of the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a seal of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it bears the signature of the gentleman that you told us about?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Jovo Banjac's signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What does it have that in your view it should have? Just pause for a moment don't answer for a moment. Wait. Wait. Sorry, Mr. Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What's it missing, Mr. Filipovic, that you saw ought to have to make it an official document?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In my opinion, in the top left corner there should be the number of the document, the date, then how it was entered into the logbook, the register book, with the seal, and then it should be said at the session held on such and such a date it is confirmed such and such, because in the files there is a logbook, a register, where each document is logged in, and it says "document X" or so on. This is what it should be. You have probably seen in some documents that this existed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Leaving aside the document at the moment itself, it refers to a decision taken in April of 1991 -- or perhaps not a decision. It refers to April 1991. Did Kljuc municipality in April 1991 join the Banja Luka Community of Municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I think so. But it says here "regional community of Bosnian Krajina." This is the Banja Luka community. We accepted to be in this region. Here you have in the second paragraph, in the regional community of Bosnian Krajina. And then further on it says "Autonomous Region." We did not wish to be part of the Autonomous Region, but we did accept to be in the Community of Municipalities. We did want to leave Jajce community of Municipalities and be part of Banja Luka Community of Municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, in the answer you gave about that, when dealing originally with the document, you mentioned Mr. Brdjanin. When did you first hear of Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Officially I first heard about Mr. Brdjanin during the pre-electoral campaign in 1990. But in fact I heard about him when word came to our institutions, Bosniak institutions. In Kljuc municipality we learnt that Mr. Brdjanin sometime in 1991 - I don't know when - signed a document asking SDS members establishment of power in the municipality. This is when I first heard and saw about him. I don't personally know him, but I've heard and saw him from TV and media.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. When you became aware of him through the TV and media, can you remember what year that was? Was it 1991 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: He was simply a person of some standing at that time. And if we watched the news on TV, if he was in a situation that something happened, his picture would appear on the screen and it said "at meeting such and such Mr. Brdjanin chaired the meeting," and then they would say what happened at that meeting, what he said personally, his speeches. I personally didn't see him. I didn't see them. I only saw it on TV or heard it on TV. It was only quoted from his speeches. Quite a long time has passed, so that I cannot give you a precise answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry. But the year. Did you first hear him quoted in 1991 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In 1991 and immediately after the elections. As soon as the power was established from 1991, as soon as something happened in the news.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that though you didn't see him live, as it were, on television, it was a report about a speech he'd made with a picture. What type of speeches was Mr. Brdjanin making?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: For instance, if we are looking at this as an example, there would be the analysis of this meeting, that -- of this session, that Serbs had to become part of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, that the only salvation for the Serb people would be to be organised in autonomous regions and so on. I cannot give you an exact quotation as to what the journalist on TV said, but this was the gist of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: From what -- and I appreciate it's a very long time ago now. From what you can remember, was there any mention by him of the other nationalities?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's leading, and I object to that. She asked him what he could remember that he said, and he told us. And she's now leading him, trying to get him to say something after he has told us what he remembers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Mr. Ackerman, I will allow the question. He's just started saying what he remembers, and it's perfectly legitimate to ask him questions to see if he could remember more. Go ahead, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, again, can you remember whether there was any mention of the other nationalities in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, for instance, I think that his mention of other nationalities -- I'm again talk about the region of Bosanska Krajina. "The Serbs have brought on the edge of biological extinction, brother Serb, we have to organise ourselves, we the Serbs --" I'm a Bosniak. I belong to the Bosniak people, and the Serbs considered that we were part of the Muslim Ustasha coalition. And when you say the Muslim Ustasha coalition which threatened them with their biological extermination, I cannot really quote the words, but the mention of other nations was roughly along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say the Muslim Ustasha coalition. Did he use the word "Ustasha"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, she -- she's totally -- he didn't say that Mr. Brdjanin said anything -- said "Muslim Ustasha coalition" or anything like that. He said -- the only thing that he heard Brdjanin talk about in the other nationalities was in connection with the Bosanska Krajina region. And then he talks about the Serbs bringing on Muslim Ustasha coalition. That's something that -- he doesn't relate to Mr. Brdjanin at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] The answer was -- he was answering --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He was answering a specific question addressed to him as to whether in these reports about the speeches of Mr. Brdjanin there were ever any reference to other nationalities in Bosnia. And he's explaining that the mention or reference to other nationalities was in the context of an alleged Muslim Ustasha coalition. This is what he is answering. That's how I understood him anyway. I mean, it's -- it's not an impression or an opinion that he formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He doesn't say that Mr. Brdjanin said anything about a Muslim Ustasha coalition. Those are -- that's his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's his analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me put -- that's how I understand him, what he was saying. Mr. Filipovic, one moment. According to the reports that you followed on the media, TV in particular, as it seems, is it your recollection that in his speeches Mr. Brdjanin made reference to a Muslim Ustasha coalition?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, he already told us that he never heard Mr. Brdjanin make a speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it's the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So he can't ask him if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: These are the reports, Mr. Ackerman. Reports. I didn't say that he -- that he ever heard Mr. Brdjanin make a speech. But he said earlier on that on TV they used to report his speeches. So. So my question to you: Is it your recollection - and you have to be very clear about this - that in these reports you heard about Mr. Brdjanin's speeches, there was a specific reference to the so-called Muslim Ustasha coalition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me answer you, Your Honour. At that time there was no Serb leader who did not mention the Muslim Ustasha coalition in his speeches. And I think that Mr. Brdjanin is one of them. You can't find any one of them who failed to mention the Muslim Ustasha coalition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is a conclusion. My question was very specific: In these reports, were the phrases, the words used, to the effect that Mr. Brdjanin had made reference, apart from the Serbs, also to the Muslim Ustasha coalition? And please answer yes or no. It's a very simple question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to make the same objection as Mr. Ackerman. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: One thing, Your Honours. Line -- page 54, line 8.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is the -- the sentence which starts "And I think."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the witness has said "I assume." He didn't say "I think." He said "Smatre" [phoen]. It is "I assume."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Is Mr. Zecevic correct, Mr. Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think and I assume and I hold that it is one in the same. I think that they're all pseudonym, different words meaning the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, that's what you recall of the reports. You told us that -- earlier that Mr. Brdjanin was one of the leaders. From what made you aware that as far as you were concerned he was one of the leaders?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: One of the documents, the one that we discussed later on, is a document that he signed, and it was about the organisation of government, of authority. While in my book, it cannot be done by a record file man. It must be somebody who holds a high office. And as far as I can remember, this document was of 1991 and then the SDA and MBO discussed this document. And I'm sure there was talk about it in the set assembly sessions, Radio Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you never met him. Do you know whether or not Mr. Banjac or Mr. Kondic or any of the other leaders of the SDS in Kljuc had any meetings with him?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they did. Because I know that -- they used the official municipal car to attend party meetings. On one occasion I even had words with my late brother, because I told him, "Why don't you request a car so that we can attend our party meetings at the state's expense." And he said, "How can we do it?" And I said, "Well, if Vinko can use it to go to Banja Luka to attend SDS meetings, then why not?" We had a meeting in Srebrenica in 1991 -- in 1991. It was already divided Stole Despotovic was the one who drove Serbs. And -- I can't remember his last name, because the man was killed, he was the man who drove the Muslims. He had a Renault. The other one had a Peugeot. And ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did your brother, the late Omer Filipovic, ever attend or meet Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: He was at a meeting. Now, I don't know whether it was in Banja Luka or perhaps Kotor Varos. But in one of those towns around Banja Luka -- or perhaps Teslic. I can't really say. But he was present at a meeting which discussed it. And after that I heard a great deal from him. He still could tell me these things. And then I heard about Brdjanin and Kupresanin and so on. But Omer did attend one of them, but I can't really say where the session was held.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, first of all, he mentioned Kupresanin. Were you aware of Mr. Kupresanin before your brother mentioned him?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Why, yes. Through the media I knew that he held an office. But the first time I saw him was at Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Of the two of them, as far as you were concerned, that is, Brdjanin and Kupresanin, who was the most public figure?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, who was the most public figure as far as you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, it was Brdjanin. But that is my personal opinion. I don't know how the government was organised, but I believe that Brdjanin was given more coverage in the news.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, finally this: When your brother came back from this meeting, wherever it was, at which Mr. Brdjanin was present, what view did he express to you as to what was going to happen in respect of the relationship between the Serb nationalities and the Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The first thing that would be done when we met - and we tried to meet in the absence of our wives and children so as not to upset them - and the first thing that we would discuss after he'd come after one of those meetings would be nothing good is in store for us. And I'd ask him why. And he'd say, "Nothing good is in store for us, same as our grandfathers, as our fathers. The same thing is in store of us. And it's only a matter of time when it will happen."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So if we summarise the position up until around October of 1991, the Bosniak parties were in agreement with joining the Community of Municipalities in Banja Luka but not when it became the Autonomous Region of Krajina. And can you just very briefly tell us why you didn't agree to become part of the Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: We did not agree to become part of the Autonomous Region of Krajina because we were aware of the concept which underlaid the organisation of that authority and that concept was that those were Serb territories only and the Serb nation was nation number 1, the Orthodox religion the religion number 1; the Cyrillic alphabet, the alphabet number 1; and quite simply whatever concern the Serb people would be number 1 and we other peoples would be second-rank peoples. And that is why we were not happy and were reluctant to join the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina, because there was nothing we could gain from the region of Bosanska Krajina. The region of Bosanska Krajina was something from, as we say in Bosnia, Tito's state. Because in Tito's time you had Jajce, Drvar, Banja Luka, everything was in working order and nobody knew -- nobody distinguished between Serbs, Croats, and Muslims. There was parity principle. If the president was a Serb, the vice-president had to be a Muslim or the secretary had to be a Croat, and that is what it came down to. However, in an autonomous region, everything from the president to the recording club, they were all supposed to be Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want then to look, please, at the next document, taking us through 1991. Could we look, please -- or could you be shown P854.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which Your Honours will find behind divider 12. Your Honours, this document is -- it's not altogether clear from the English, anyhow -- was part of Radio Kljuc broadcast. It's not objected to, and it was given by the local AID office.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's dated the 25th of June, Mr. Filipovic, and it talks about a public discussion in the community centre that you've identified with Professor Muhamed Filipovic. And that's the gentleman you identified as your relative; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It -- I don't want to go through the whole document because it's just this -- because it refers to the secession of Yugoslavia from Slovinia and Croatia and the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina. What effect did the secession of these two parts of -- republics of Yugoslavia have on the atmosphere in Kljuc itself?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The secession of Slovenia and Croatia from Yugoslavia affected the atmosphere in Kljuc because all citizens in Kljuc - and I should say all the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina - held that Yugoslavia was sustainable only within its own boundaries, that is, including Slovenia and Croatia, that there could be no Yugoslavia without Slovenia and Croatia. And all further efforts were aimed at showing that it was not Yugoslavia any more. We -- there was even a term "rump Yugoslavia." But we couldn't agree with this rump Yugoslavia because there was no Yugoslavia without Slovenia and Croatia. And Slovenia, it seems, were much too easily allowed to leave Yugoslavia, and we Bosnians refused it, so that this meeting was about this, whether we should remain in the rump Yugoslavia or should we also pursue the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, because Yugoslavia within the boundaries as established by Marsal Josip Broz Tito was Yugoslavia which suited best us Muslims, that is, Bosniaks. We wanted to live in that Yugoslavia, and at no point in time did we try to break it apart. I come from a prominent family, from a big family, from an aristocratic family which lost a great deal in that Yugoslavia by dealing with all sorts of reforms. But we were happy with that Yugoslavia. We were content with it because we were appreciated the world over. With that passport we could go all over the world. And now we cannot make a single step without a visa. So we, the Bosnians, Muslims, we were quite content and at no time did we try to undermine Yugoslavia. But we did not think that if Slovenia was allowed to leave and part of Croatia, then it wouldn't be Yugoslavia, because we knew that even in the project it was envisaged when, where the boundaries of Greater Serbia should be, and that is Karlovac and all that there. And the latest war in Bosnia had shown that the front lines followed the boundaries where the politician Moljevic saw the borders of Greater Serbia, and we simply couldn't come to terms to living in Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want to move then please on -- and if you could turn to the next -- if you could be given, rather, the next document, which is pre-marked P855. And it follows straight on in the bundle. It's a document which is headed "Statement," and dated, we can see at the bottom, the 19th of July. And again, it comes from Radio Kljuc, Your Honours. It's handwritten, "Serbian Orthodox Church Kljuc," and it says: "In July and August 1941, a terrible crime was committed against innocent, helpless, and humiliated Serbian people in the school in Kljuc -- Vrhpolje. For 50 years we failed heed the mysterious message of their graves and we owe it to their sacrifices to interpret history fairly." Then there's a reference to a memorial service on the 2nd of August and a bit more rhetoric, if I can put it that way, calling people to come. Now, these types of announcements affected -- recalling the events of 1941, was this happening rarely or quite a lot at this period of time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, please. I'm sorry. I'm sorry, Mr. Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: This document shows that the Serb Orthodox Church and the Serb Democratic Party acted together.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I must object. The question was asked -- was very simple: "Was this happening rarely or quite a lot?" He's now going into some long explanation of the document. And the question is "Is this rare or not?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Objection sustained. Mr. Filipovic, the question was: "Now, these types of announcements --" the question was whether these were -- let me find the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I remember the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. What -- just answer yes or no, whether it was rarely or quite a lot.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite a lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But as a man, I should answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to ask you the --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: This is not all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you can answer the question you're asked and then I'll ask a -- I'll ask some follow-up questions on that. So the answer was happening quite a lot. You say this show it is connection between the Orthodox Church and the Serbian -- the SDS. And I think the answer is obvious, but why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I say it because of a press release that was sent to the local radio. And on one and the same sheet of paper two institutions, that is, the Serb Orthodox Church and the Serb Democratic Party co-signed this press release. There should be two different press releases. But as a witness, I'd like to explain this invitation to the service by the SPS and the SDS, as said. Because it is always said that in World War II the Serbs were slaughtered, but nobody came up with the thesis how is it that people were killed in World War II. The truth which could never be told in public is that members of Ante Pavelic's army entered Kljuc --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, the Chamber is not interested in a historical explanation of the events of World War II. Please -- I'm stopping the witness now. Ask him a further question which changes the subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I think the answer -- Your Honour, I think for this limited purpose alone, because it refers to a terrible crime committed against the people of Kljuc. And I can deal with that very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But on the same score, we in Malta, we wouldn't be on -- wouldn't be talking terms with the Germans, with the French, with the Italians, with no one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, there's a slight difference. But I can deal with it very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, just very briefly - and as you heard His Honour, we don't need a dissertation on World War II -- but this was recalling to mind what was alleged to be a crime. Very briefly can you tell us what they were referring to in this announcement.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: They are referring to a communication that several Serbs were killed in those places in Kljuc, and they accused the Muslims of it. But the truth is that those Serbs were killed by members of the Ante -- of Ante Pavelic's army, who entered Kljuc, put on their fezzes, that is the ethnic cap of Muslims. And instead of being called Jure, Frane, or whatever, they assumed the names of Mujo, Suljo, and this Serb idea, that they have to avenge the death and on Muslims, because the Muslims had allegedly killed them. But it has been proven that that crime was committed by members of Ante Pavelic's troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, the only other question is: How often were the events of the Second World War being brought up in Kljuc in this period in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Every address. Every speech by a member of the SDS, either in public venues or political meetings they would -- when they would always start talking "What did the Muslim Ustasha coalition do to us?" That was always the beginning of every speech because that is their chief motif, that is how they tried to involve the rest of the Serb masses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Then perhaps before the break I can deal with one further document. And for that we need to go back. And could you be hand P852, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's behind divider 10.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is an official statement issued by the MBO municipal board in Kljuc. It's undated, but it states the following: "In agreement with the SDA, that there's been psychological pressure on the Muslim population, that --" and I'm going to skip the first three paragraphs. Paragraph 4: "The rumours have now turned into concrete threats in the form of anonymous letters to prominent figures of Muslim political life. The best example is a letter that Omer Filipovic received on the 8th of May this year which disparaged the political, religious, and cultural sentiments of the Muslims in a vulgar way and made direct threats of the use of Chetnik methods." And then it goes on to state that "The MBO and the SDA in Kljuc will represent the interests of the Muslim people and also the interests of peace and co-existence." And then finally it talks about the establishment of a patriotic civic front. And again, I think -- I'll just check that, that this document was Radio Kljuc. Now, first of all, it's not dated. From what's in there, are you able to give us a rough date of when this was issued?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Which document do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: P852, this one that you're look at?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: This one here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: This, I'd say it was issued sometime in May, because I've already said in the beginning that we all did it at our own expense. That is, we covered -- we bore all the expenses ourselves. So when we came by some paper, then we would write a document and submit it to the Radio Kljuc at the session of the MBO held on such and such date.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And that is how we sent it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'm just trying to establish -- May 1991 or May 1992 it talks about a patriotic civic front.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So does that make it May 1991 or May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: It can't be 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Because in May 1992 there was a war on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So in May of 1991 --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I guess so because as of the 7th of May, 1992 the crisis started. It was when the Serb police took over.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, then two questions about this document. First of all, it talks about an initiative for the establishment of a patriotic civic front. What was that going to be?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Our intention was to gather all inhabitants of Kljuc who were pro-Bosnian. We were not interested in ethnicity or religion. But all inhabitants who is had Bosnia-Herzegovina in their hearts, to gather them and to attempt through a reasonable discussion, a reasonable debate, to convince them what would happen and to each try and do something to stop the threat of war which was hovering over Kljuc and over the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It refers in paragraph 4 to a letter that was received by your brother. Did your brother -- well, first of all, your brother. Did your brother receive one letter or more than one letter?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: My brother received several letters; so did I. We had telephone threats, threats in the street when we were stopped occasionally. It happened. At any moment there would be a threat. We would go to sleep at night and the telephone would ring. There would be a threat that our house would be blown up. But we were not frightened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, when you returned to Kljuc in, I think, 1996, did you find an example of the type of letter that your brother was getting?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd like you to have a look, please --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a new document. I think Your Honour has been provided with a copy. It bears the ERN number 02133004. Can you give it to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we'll stop here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to deal with this letter and nothing else, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's undated, but from the contents we can tell that it came later than 1991. And does it read as follows: "Omer, you balija, 400 of my men are in Vrbanja, Gornji Ratkovo, and Bravsko. This is because of your behaviour towards the Serbian people and the setting up of barricades in Pudin Han, Krasulje, Ramici, and Biljani. Under the command of Vojvoda -- which means "military leader" apparently -- Vojislav Seselj We have organised a detachment of Chetnik volunteers which is headquartered in Gornji Ratkovo. We'll fuck your Ustasha mother. We'll piss on the Croatian chequer-board and the Muslim crescent. Western Serbia, the illegal Serbian Chetnik movement [As read]." Now, were the other letters that your brother and you received couched -- expressed in the same terms?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The terms were more or less the same. The only thing that I would say is that Vojvoda is not a military leader. It's just a Chetnik title. It's the highest thing that a Chetnik could be, a Vojvoda. It's not a rank.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, could that be made Prosecutor's Exhibit -- 1099, I'm told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we need to stop here for the day. We will resume our -- on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The witness, Your Honour, I think at quarter to 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But I suppose that we need to explain to you. We will be starting -- continuing with your evidence on Monday at -- and not at quarter past 2.00 but at quarter past 3.00 because --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Quarter to 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Quarter to 3.00, sorry, because before you come in we need to discuss a procedural matter, which we have postponing from today. In the meantime, please do try to have the transcript of whatever you needed to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, can I tell Your Honour that arrangements have been made. The transcript will be available on Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's perfect.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In the light of Mr. Ackerman's suggestion, though, I don't think it's possible to have a legal discussion without Your Honours looking at it. But I'll have it available at court and then we can discuss that part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The hearing will be at 2.15. Yes, the hearing will be at 2.15. It's only the witness that need not be brought to stay in the room an hour before. You know, I mean, it's -- so good afternoon to everyone. Thank you. And have a nice weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 12.07 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday the 2nd day of September, 2002, at 2.15 p.m.
